clue.text: Cash (both extremes) described by newspaper articles – like so?

definitions.text: Cash (both extremes) described by newspaper articles – like so?

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, so only those two are kept
to describe is to draw a line around, so the cash letters sit inside the articles

blocks.note: first and last letters of cash
rag is slang for a low-grade newspaper
newspaper articles are stories

explanation.surface: A newspaper feature about money, presented with a wink as an example of itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is its own definition: tabloid stories about someone suddenly coming into money are the classic rags-to-riches tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A rags-to-riches tale is the classic story of sudden wealth, exactly what newspaper pieces about cash coming into a life describe.

clue.text: Another hearing it, rare rare owl’s back

indicators.note: the second rare is read as unusual, telling us the preceding letters come out in an unusual order
the back of a word is its final letter, so only that one is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder
last letter of owl

explanation.surface: Someone at a hearing reports an owl's rear end, absurdly rare twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubled 'rare' looks like a typo or stutter; the first is fodder, the second the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A retrial is a second trial of the same case, so it is another hearing in court.

clue.text: Measure of corporation in hindsight, rightfully upset

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the words that follow
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from the bottom up

blocks.note: the end of hindsight running into the start of rightfully

explanation.surface: A company's size judged in hindsight, and the verdict rightly overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporation is the jokey word for a big belly, not a company.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth is the measurement around the middle, so it is how a paunch, or corporation, is sized up.

clue.text: Killing in order, not everyone for the dictator?

indicators.note: a dictator here is someone dictating out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: neat and in order
some means not all

explanation.surface: A tyrant sets out a killing list neatly, though not everyone is on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Dictator is not a tyrant but someone dictating a letter, so a spoken word is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a killing is earning a big profit, and a tidy sum is a large amount of money.

clue.text: Body, jeepers, exuded fluid!

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like jeepers
fluid oozing from an infection

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in disgust at a body oozing fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpus is Latin for body and is used in English for a body of writings or a physical body.

clue.text: Number one in head after zero

indicators.note: in places the one letter inside the word for head
after says the head piece follows the zero piece

blocks.note: zero looks like the letter O
Roman numeral one
pate is an old word for the head

explanation.surface: Being number one but coming after a zero.
explanation.walkthrough: Number is read as something that numbs, not a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: An opiate dulls pain and feeling, so it is a drug that numbs: a number.

clue.text: Game of cards, simple game where hand thrown in

indicators.note: game can mean lame or damaged, as in a game leg, so the letters are out of shape
something thrown in goes into the middle of the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder
a hand is a worker, and to man something is to staff it

explanation.surface: A simple card game where players throw in their hands.
explanation.walkthrough: PELMANISM is the memory game of turning up cards to find pairs, also called pairs or concentration.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelmanism is a card game in which face-down cards are turned over two at a time to find matching pairs.

clue.text: Shriek having lost a companion – it sounds like it sucks

indicators.note: having lost says a letter goes missing from the shriek word

blocks.note: a high-pitched cry
the letter that is lost
Companion of Honour, a British order, abbreviated CH

explanation.surface: A scream after a friend is lost, and a sucking noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like a homophone signal, but it is describing a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A squelch is the wet sucking noise of boots in mud, a sound that suggests suction.

clue.text: Whitehall greed with African trips, that cargo needs protection!

indicators.note: trips means stumbles, so the letters tumble into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Greedy civil servants on African jaunts, with a warning about precious freight.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitehall is the London street of government ministries, standing for the civil service.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the label stuck on breakable freight, warning carriers to treat the load gently.

clue.text: Sun with dawn briefly seen

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: the dawn of something is its start

explanation.surface: The sun appearing at daybreak.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun is a star, the nearest one to Earth, so it is an example of the class.

clue.text: Mechanism on bike all rider has used, oddly, when changing

indicators.note: oddly keeps the letters in odd-numbered positions of the word before
changing means altering, so the gathered letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
first and third letters of used

explanation.surface: Every cyclist relies on this part when changing gear.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface 'changing' fits gears perfectly, hiding its job as the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A derailleur is the gear-shifting device on a bicycle that moves the chain between sprockets.

clue.text: See 1
Take a seat in restaurant, perhaps, not beyond solver?

blocks.note: to take is to get
in a restaurant you sit at a table

explanation.surface: Booking a seat at a restaurant, and wondering if the solver can manage it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gettable can be obtained or understood, so a clue that is not beyond the solver is within reach.

clue.text: Llama and ape scrapping, in goes hard chest-beating primate

indicators.note: scrapping means fighting, and brawling animals end up in a jumble

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A llama and an ape fighting, and a gorilla barges in thumping its chest.
explanation.definitionFit: The alpha male is the dominant animal in a primate group, the one that beats its chest to assert power.

clue.text: Wonder if not immediately apparent in fridge magnet?

definitions.text: Wonder if not immediately apparent in fridge magnet?

blocks.note: something not obvious at first is concealed
a gem is a marvel, a treasure

explanation.surface: Pondering whether a fridge magnet hides something wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue demonstrates itself: the word for a wonder really is concealed across the end of fridge and the start of magnet.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden gem is an excellent thing that few people notice, a marvel not obvious at first.

clue.text: See 8 Down
Wait, POTU?

blocks.note: POTUS, the US president's title, cut short: so the then president's name is cut short too

explanation.surface: Waiting on the US president, misspelt.
explanation.walkthrough: POTUS (President of the United States) appears without its last letter, so the president of 2024, Biden, loses his last letter too.
explanation.definitionFit: To bide is to wait, as in biding your time.

clue.text: Action that brings up taste in food?

definitions.text: Action that brings up taste in food?

indicators.note: in places the taste word inside the food word
in a down clue bringing up raises the letters so they read from the bottom

blocks.note: grub is informal for food
a nip is a small taste of drink

explanation.surface: A food critic's habit of raising the matter of flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: belching brings the taste of a meal back up.
explanation.definitionFit: Belching after a meal releases gas and with it a reminder of the food's flavour.

clue.text: A sign of the swine being completed by cruciverbalist, finally – eureka!

indicators.note: finally points at the last letter of the word before

blocks.note: taken as written
ham comes from the pig
an omen is a sign of things to come
last letter of cruciverbalist

explanation.surface: A crossword setter finally cracks a pig-related clue and shouts eureka.
explanation.walkthrough: A cruciverbalist is a crossword enthusiast. 'Of the swine' gives the meat that comes before the sign in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eureka is the cry of sudden discovery, and an aha moment is that instant of insight.

clue.text: Bomb owed, declared however

indicators.note: declared means spoken out, so the words are taken by sound

blocks.note: a mine is a buried bomb, and what is owed is due

explanation.surface: A bomb that someone was owed, announced with a qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: Mind you is a spoken qualifier introducing a contrast, just as however does.

clue.text: Turn to specious note – that’s what it is?

definitions.text: Turn to specious note – that’s what it is?

indicators.note: specious means falsely plausible, so the letters are presented in a misleading order

blocks.note: taken as written
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A warning against relying on a misleading memo.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole clue: something specious is, by definition, false, so 'that's what it is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Specious means plausible but false, so what a specious note says is false.

clue.text: Intended to give tips on cabriole after simple lifts

indicators.note: in a down clue lifts means raised, so the word reads from the bottom up
the tips of a word are its two ends
after places the tips behind the raised word

blocks.note: naif means naive or unsophisticated
first and last letters of cabriole

explanation.surface: A ballet dancer's intended cabriole leap after simple lifts.
explanation.walkthrough: A cabriole is a ballet jump, so lifts look like part of the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: One's intended is the person one plans to marry, which is what a fiancé is.

clue.text: Ears ain’t in need of treatment – so well?

definitions.note: adjective describing a well; 'so' says the answer is a kind of well

indicators.note: something needing treatment is in poor shape, so the letters must be put right

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone insists their ears don't need treatment, so they're fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' reads as healthy, but it is a hole in the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: An artesian well is a bored well where water rises under its own natural pressure.

clue.text: Exposure of song just written for the radio?

indicators.note: on the radio words are only heard, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: a ditty is a short song, and one just written is new

explanation.surface: A fresh song written for broadcast, with a scandalous exposure.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecent exposure is the showing of the naked body, and nudity is that state of nakedness.

clue.text: Ailing – like a detective?

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for weak or unsound, as in a dodgy heart
second meaning: a dick is slang for a detective, so this is a jokey adjective from it

explanation.walkthrough: Dicky is informal British for poorly or unreliable, as in a dicky tummy; the question mark flags the invented sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Dicky is British slang for unwell or faulty, and the pun links it to dick, an American word for private eye.

clue.text: Flirt cut by villain with end of weapon – as slash seen?

indicators.note: cut by means split open by, so the flirting word is broken apart with letters inside
end of takes just the final letter of the next word

blocks.note: to dally is to toy amorously
Iago, the schemer in Shakespeare's Othello
last letter of weapon

explanation.surface: A flirt slashed by a knife-wielding villain.
explanation.walkthrough: Slash is the punctuation mark, not a knife wound.
explanation.definitionFit: The slash punctuation mark is a stroke that leans at an angle, running on a slant across the line.

clue.text: See 8 Down
Boring thing, jacketed male?

indicators.note: something jacketed is wrapped in an outer garment

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for male
a gilet is a sleeveless jacket

explanation.surface: A dull man in a smart jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacketed both supplies the garment and says it goes round.
explanation.definitionFit: A gimlet is a small hand tool for drilling holes, so it bores, which makes it a boring thing.

clue.text: Veep unfamiliar with King Edward, game for the reporter?

indicators.note: a reporter speaks the story, so the word is chosen by its sound

blocks.note: quail is a game bird

explanation.surface: A US vice president who doesn't know a British monarch, game for a press interview.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward is a British potato variety; Dan Quayle, US vice president, famously misspelt potato as 'potatoe' in 1992.
explanation.definitionFit: Dan Quayle was the American vice president, or veep, mocked for his blunder spelling the vegetable.
